parts.transcript: Hello everyone, my name is Jane. I am here on behalf of the San Martin Zoo to tell you about my job as a zoologist. Over the years, many people have asked me how I first obtained my interest in zoology. Some people presume that I got into it by buying a pet from the pet store or by watching a lot of TV programs about animals. But, in fact, I first realized I had an interest in caring for animals when I was 12 years old. My father brought home an injured baby kangaroo that he found alongside the road after it had been hit by a car. I spent about six weeks nursing it to good health and then released it into the wild again. As a young girl, I had never saved a life before. After gaining the experience, I realized that I loved spending my time caring for animals. It was very rewarding. Well, you may be curious about how I managed to acquire knowledge about animals. I have been so lucky to get the first-hand knowledge from many of my workmates here, and I really appreciate their help. Though, I have learned something from the books I read before and the teachers in primary school also inspired me at times. I have routine work to do on a daily basis. Sometimes I may get temporary work. For example, I occasionally collect food for the animals and sometimes care for the injured ones. But I spend most of my working time keeping all the animals well-fed and nourished. As zoo workers, we hope all animals are healthy. Working in the zoo is never an easy job. It requires you to be absolutely patient since you are with animals and you have to be fit enough to do some physically demanding work. For me, I like to teach animals how to react to specific conditions or stimuli, even though sometimes the young ones are so naughty that they can drive you mad. Caring for injured animals is also part of my work, and I derive the most delight and pleasure from doing so, especially when I see them restoring to good health. So far, I have saved some animals' lives and I take great pride in having done that. Caring for newborn babies is relatively a relaxing part of this work. The most important thing is that I should always be careful as they are very vulnerable to all types of disease. Now we have enough staff working as guides who will show the visitors around. Many volunteers have asked about the job related to raising animals, I am afraid that we won't need more hands until December. But since some of our show planners are on a business trip, it would be great if there are some people who can fill this vacancy. As you listen to me talking about zoos, you may be wondering what the main role of a zoo is. Well, zoos are all set to protect some species from any forms of harm. And we also spend time doing research about animals. We do these things because we want to teach our visitors something about the animals in the zoo, rather than just make money from tickets. In doing this, we hope to get them involved in preserving the species or caring for the habitats of the species. We try to lay the groundwork for this by encouraging kids to become involved at the zoo, and I am glad that it works. Many children are calling us, asking if there is any position for volunteers. Since it's not peak season, we only have part-time work. If you are interested in zoology or you want to spend some time with animals, you are always welcome. For those who are not sure if they can do this kind of work, I suggest you can first try to give food to some native animals to experience what it is like to be with animals. We are aware that for students, apart from learning about animals from books whenever possible, observation is a good way to acquire knowledge as well. And then, for those who want to learn even more about animals, our senior workmates who have worked at the zoo for at least three years are always willing to tell you all about animal breeding. My associates and I are readily available to share our knowledge with any of you who are interested. Thank you for your time and attention today. Please know that I am now available to answer any questions you might have regarding zoology or our San Martin Zoo. Thank you for coming. Have a great day!

questions.transcript: Hello everyone, my name is Jane. I am here on behalf of the San Martin Zoo to tell you about my job as a zoologist. Over the years, many people have asked me how I first obtained my interest in zoology. Some people presume that I got into it by buying a pet from the pet store or by watching a lot of TV programs about animals. But, in fact, I first realized I had an interest in caring for animals when I was 12 years old. My father brought home an injured baby kangaroo that he found alongside the road after it had been hit by a car. I spent about six weeks nursing it to good health and then released it into the wild again. As a young girl, I had never saved a life before. After gaining the experience, I realized that I loved spending my time caring for animals. It was very rewarding. Well, you may be curious about how I managed to acquire knowledge about animals. I have been so lucky to get the first-hand knowledge from many of my workmates here, and I really appreciate their help. Though, I have learned something from the books I read before and the teachers in primary school also inspired me at times. I have routine work to do on a daily basis. Sometimes I may get temporary work. For example, I occasionally collect food for the animals and sometimes care for the injured ones. But I spend most of my working time keeping all the animals well-fed and nourished. As zoo workers, we hope all animals are healthy. Working in the zoo is never an easy job. It requires you to be absolutely patient since you are with animals and you have to be fit enough to do some physically demanding work. For me, I like to teach animals how to react to specific conditions or stimuli, even though sometimes the young ones are so naughty that they can drive you mad. Caring for injured animals is also part of my work, and I derive the most delight and pleasure from doing so, especially when I see them restoring to good health. So far, I have saved some animals' lives and I take great pride in having done that. Caring for newborn babies is relatively a relaxing part of this work. The most important thing is that I should always be careful as they are very vulnerable to all types of disease. Now we have enough staff working as guides who will show the visitors around. Many volunteers have asked about the job related to raising animals, I am afraid that we won't need more hands until December. But since some of our show planners are on a business trip, it would be great if there are some people who can fill this vacancy. As you listen to me talking about zoos, you may be wondering what the main role of a zoo is. Well, zoos are all set to protect some species from any forms of harm. And we also spend time doing research about animals. We do these things because we want to teach our visitors something about the animals in the zoo, rather than just make money from tickets. In doing this, we hope to get them involved in preserving the species or caring for the habitats of the species. We try to lay the groundwork for this by encouraging kids to become involved at the zoo, and I am glad that it works. Many children are calling us, asking if there is any position for volunteers. Since it's not peak season, we only have part-time work. If you are interested in zoology or you want to spend some time with animals, you are always welcome. For those who are not sure if they can do this kind of work, I suggest you can first try to give food to some native animals to experience what it is like to be with animals. We are aware that for students, apart from learning about animals from books whenever possible, observation is a good way to acquire knowledge as well. And then, for those who want to learn even more about animals, our senior workmates who have worked at the zoo for at least three years are always willing to tell you all about animal breeding. My associates and I are readily available to share our knowledge with any of you who are interested. Thank you for your time and attention today. Please know that I am now available to answer any questions you might have regarding zoology or our San Martin Zoo. Thank you for coming. Have a great day!

parts.transcript: Hi Linda, can you spare a few minutes? Hello Matthew, no problem. I just wanted to talk to you about temporary work placements. I’ve never really thought there was a good reason for doing one. I’ve got some savings so I don’t really need the money at the moment, but I’ve had an email from the university about a vacancy that looks quite interesting. You did a placement last year, didn’t you? I did, yes. In my case, I wanted to find out if I was making the right career choice before I began applying for permanent jobs. I thought I wanted to work in car manufacturing, but I wasn’t sure, so I applied to Toyota. What was the application process like? Lengthy. There were a lot of different parts to it. The dullest one was a psychometric test. You know, when you have to answer loads of questions about yourself… And you’re trying to guess what’s the best thing to say. Yes. Then there was an activity that we did in groups, which I found really fascinating. Engineers are renowned for being a bit unsociable, but I thought we made a great team. And we had an individual task too. We had to sort through various business documents and prioritize them. It was just like what you have to do as a student, really, just with different content. What exactly were you doing on the placement? I was helping to design some diagnostic software to identify any waste in the car assembly process. Do you mean waste of materials? No, time. Anything that can speed the process up helps to cut costs. How did the work placement compare to being a student? Was it hard work? Yes, it was. I’d had full-time work before. I’ve done various unskilled jobs during university holidays, and some of those involve long hours. So I thought I’d find it easy. I was wrong, though. I think when you’re on placement, you’re always trying to prove yourself. So you push yourself hard to succeed. Yes. But I got a lot of support from my employers. They were always helpful. And then at the end of the placement, I was given formal feedback. Do you mean on your engineering ability? Well, no, I didn’t really need that because we had team meetings every other day, and so I had the chance to discuss technical issues and ask about anything that wasn’t clear. The evaluation was about general workplace things, like organizational ability, initiative, that sort of thing. I get the impression you think you benefited from the placement. Well, the best thing is that they’ve offered me a job for next year, depending on my exam results, of course, but still — a permanent one. Yes, but apart from that, I learned so much. The industrial environment was much more demanding than the academic one, so my general skills improved, like time management, meeting deadlines, and on the technical side, I learned new software packages like MS Project. Well, I think you’ve convinced me that work placements are worthwhile, but — while you’re here, can you give me advice on something else? I’m about to make a start on the engineering materials module, and I’ve got a book list here. Can you have a quick look and tell me what you would recommend? That’s if you can remember. Let’s see. task1.title: Task 1: Formal / Semi-formal Letter
task1.prompt: You recently stayed at a hotel on an official business trip and encountered several problems during your stay. Write a formal letter to the hotel manager. In your letter: explain why you were staying at the hotel, describe the problems you experienced, and state what actions you expect the manager to take.
task1.sampleBand8Answer:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to formally register my disappointment regarding the quality of accommodation during my stay at the Grand Imperial Hotel from October 18th to October 21st (Booking Reference: #GI-98421). I was visiting your city as the keynote speaker at the International Energy Symposium.

Regrettably, multiple deficiencies compromised what ought to have been a restful business visit. First, despite confirming a high-floor executive quiet room weeks prior, I was assigned Room 204 adjacent to the main loading dock, where delivery freight commenced noisily at 5:00 AM each morning. Furthermore, the high-speed Wi-Fi connection advertised in the executive suite failed intermittently throughout my stay, preventing me from accessing critical presentation materials for my conference.

To compound these issues, when I raised these urgent concerns with the front desk duty supervisor on the morning of October 19th, the staff member appeared dismissive and failed to offer an alternative room or technical support.

In light of these inconveniences and the substandard service rendered, I request a refund of 50% of the total accommodation fee charged to my corporate card. Additionally, I would appreciate a written assurance detailing the measures you intend to institute to improve staff responsiveness and internet stability.

I look forward to receiving your prompt resolution.

Yours faithfully,
Dr. Jonathan Miller

task2.title: Task 2: General Essay
task2.prompt: In many countries today, people are spending less time with their families and more time at work or pursuing individual hobbies. What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on society?
task2.sampleBand8Answer:
In contemporary society, an increasing number of individuals devote an overwhelming proportion of their daily lives to workplace commitments and autonomous pastimes, resulting in a noticeable decline in familial interaction. This essay will examine the primary catalysts behind this phenomenon and discuss its profound ramifications for community cohesion.

The primary impetus behind diminishing family time is escalating economic pressure and the competitive nature of the globalized job market. With housing costs and general living expenses soaring in metropolitan hubs, adults frequently find themselves obliged to work excessive overtime or manage secondary freelance gigs to attain financial stability. Concurrently, the pervasive presence of personalized digital entertainment—such as algorithmic social media and on-demand streaming—encourages solitary engagement rather than collective domestic pastimes.

Regarding the impacts, this societal transition generates considerable adverse repercussions. Within the household, the lack of parental presence and meaningful communication can weaken intergenerational bonding, leaving children vulnerable to behavioral issues and emotional isolation. At a broader societal level, the erosion of cohesive family structures diminishes the collective resilience of communities, as strong domestic units have traditionally served as the initial safety net during psychological and financial crises.

In summary, intense corporate demands and digital individualism represent the chief reasons why people are drifting from domestic life. Unless societies institute sustainable work-life balance policies, familial ties and social well-being will continue to erode.

part2.title: Part 2: Individual Long Turn / Cue Card (3-4 mins)

cueCard.prompt: Describe a memorable professional or academic achievement that you are proud of.
bullets: When and where it took place
What challenges you had to overcome
And explain why you felt so proud of this accomplishment.

part2.sampleBand8Answer:
I would like to speak about a defining professional achievement from last year, when I successfully spearheaded the migration of our company's legacy customer management infrastructure to a secure cloud platform. This undertaking occurred over a grueling six-month period at our regional corporate headquarters.

The primary obstacle we confronted was the sheer complexity of legacy data formats, compounded by an unforgiving deployment deadline. We had to ensure zero downtime for over fifty thousand active global clients while synchronizing disparate legacy databases. Furthermore, midway through the project, several senior specialists had to quarantine due to seasonal health issues, which forced me to shoulder additional architectural duties and coordinate with offshore teams across multiple time zones.

Ultimately, the migration went live seamlessly without a single minute of service disruption. I felt immensely proud not only because the project cut infrastructure overhead by thirty percent, but because it substantiated my leadership capabilities under immense pressure and earned our team formal recognition from executive leadership.
